title: Beneath your feet
hook: a tree that fills your arms grows from a tiny shoot; a thousand-mile journey starts beneath your feet (Tao Te Ching 64)

segments.voice: Yesterday, great things while small: the knot picked loose before it pulls tight. Your line was while it's small. What little thing did you catch in time? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step. It's the sort of line that ends up on a coffee mug, or a poster over a desk, or a graduation card. And it comes from chapter sixty-four of the Tao Te Ching. But the Chinese line doesn't quite say step. It says the journey begins beneath the feet. That small difference moves the starting line. It isn't out there, one stride away. It's under you, right now, wherever you're sitting. Today, beneath your feet.
screen: `A LINE FOR A COFFEE MUG.` → `NOT QUITE A STEP.` → `BENEATH YOUR FEET.`

segments.voice: First, three growing things. The chapter lines them up. In James Legge's translation: "The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout." Then a tower of nine stories that rose from a heap of earth. Then the journey of a thousand li, a Chinese measure of distance. Each one is huge at the end and tiny at the start. Second, where the journey begins. The Chinese phrase is short: it begins below the foot. Legge renders it "commenced with a single step," which is how the mug got its line. But the picture underneath is plainer. Not a heroic first stride. Just the ground under your shoes, the place you already are. Third, a warning near the end of the chapter. People, it says, often ruin a thing when it's almost done. So be as careful at the end as at the beginning, and nothing will be spoiled. The long journey can fail on the last mile as easily as the first. Fourth, the chair you're in. The thing you've been meaning to start, the letter, the class, the conversation, the cleared-out closet, doesn't begin on some better morning, in some better mood. It begins from this chair, this kitchen, this hour, with whatever is already in reach. The tree didn't wait to be big. It was a sprout first, exactly where it stood.
screen: `A SPROUT, A HEAP, A JOURNEY.` · `IT STARTS BENEATH YOUR FEET.` · `CAREFUL AT THE END, TOO.` · then, large: `THE GROUND YOU'RE ON NOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take the first step of something. Sit with both feet flat on the floor and feel them there. The weight. The ground pushing back. Let your breath settle into that contact. Now name one thing you've been meaning to begin. Keep it real and keep it small. Then ask: what's the first piece that can happen from exactly where I'm sitting? Not tomorrow. Not after the right mood. From here. Let the answer come, and when it does, rest your attention back in your feet. When the bell rings, that piece is beneath them. The bell holds the time.
Beneath your feet. In chapter sixty-four, the journey of a thousand li begins below the foot, right where you stand. Today's word.
Your line: beneath my feet. Start one thing today from exactly where you are, with what's already in reach. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter sixty-four as a reminder to begin large things with the small step at hand, and to stay careful right through to the end.
